name: Which practical questions arise when training an MLP by gradient descent, and which issues of the error surface complicate the descent (local minima, weight-space symmetry, saddle points, flat regions, steep cliffs, local vs. global structure)?
answer:
Practical questions.
Training efficiency: what size of a minibatch? How to choose the learning rate \(\varepsilon(t)\) and control SGD? How to pre-process the inputs? How to initialize the weights? How to choose the desired output values of the network?
Quality of the resulting model: when to stop training? Regularization techniques. How large a network?
(The reasoning is illustrated on an MLP with mse; other topologies and error functions have different but related issues.)

Issues in gradient descent.
• Local minima: small networks have lots of local minima where the descent gets stuck. Recent studies show that for sufficiently large networks all local minima have low values of the error function.
• Model identifiability – weight-space symmetry: permuting two hidden neurons of one layer together with all their incoming and outgoing weights (and biases) gives a different weight vector that computes exactly the same function. Hence many different weight vectors represent the same network function, and the error surface contains many equivalent copies of every minimum. (Swapping only the incoming weights of two neurons would in general change the function – the outgoing weights must be swapped too; the informal phrase "swap incoming weights" is imprecise.)
• Saddle points: one can show (by a combinatorial argument) that larger networks have exponentially more saddle points than local minima.
• Too slow descent – flat regions: the gradient is tiny on plateaus, so the steps are very small.
• Too fast descent – steep cliffs: the gradient is extremely large, and the descent skips important weight vectors (it jumps far away from the region where it was making progress).
• Local vs. global structure: the local shape of the error function may not point towards a good solution. For example, if the error is flat or rises on one side of a hill and the low-error region lies behind the hill, a descent initialized on the wrong side follows the local gradient and never gets over the hill.
keyPoints: Efficiency: minibatch size, learning rate, preprocessing, initialization; quality: stopping, regularization, network size
Small networks: many local minima; large networks: local minima have low error
Weight-space symmetry: permuting hidden neurons with all their incoming and outgoing weights keeps the function
Saddle points exponentially more frequent than local minima in larger networks
Flat regions → too slow; steep cliffs → huge gradient skips good weights
Local structure may mislead (descent started on the wrong side of a hill)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 103–107 (slide 104 says "swapping incoming weights"; the corrected symmetry statement is derived; the hill example is described in words)

name: Roughly, what does the theorem on gradient descent in large networks say? State its assumptions and conclusion.
answer:
Theorem (roughly). Assume:
• activation functions: "smooth" ReLU (softplus) \(\sigma(z)=\log(1+\exp(z))\); in general smooth, non-polynomial, analytic, Lipschitz continuous;
• data: inputs \(x_k\) of Euclidean norm equal to 1, desired values \(d_k\) such that all \(\lvert d_k\rvert\) are bounded by a constant;
• width: the number of hidden neurons per layer is sufficiently large – polynomial in certain numerical characteristics of the inputs (roughly measuring their similarity) and exponential in the depth of the network;
• learning rate: constant and sufficiently small.

Then gradient descent converges (with high probability w.r.t. the random initialization) to a global minimum with zero error at a linear rate.

Remark: for a special type of network called ResNet (later in the course) the result demands only polynomially many neurons per layer w.r.t. the depth.

Meaning (interpretation): although the error function is non-convex, sufficiently wide (over-parametrised) networks can be trained to zero training error by plain gradient descent – consistent with the observation that large networks do not suffer from bad local minima.
keyPoints: Smooth activations (e.g. softplus \(\log(1+e^z)\))
Unit-norm inputs, bounded desired values
Very wide layers: polynomial in data characteristics, exponential in depth
Constant, sufficiently small learning rate
GD converges w.h.p. to a global minimum with zero error at a linear rate
ResNet: only polynomial width in depth needed
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 108 (the closing "Meaning" remark is an interpretation)

name: What are the issues in computing the gradient (vanishing/exploding gradients, inexact minibatch gradients), and what considerations determine the choice of the minibatch size?
answer:
Vanishing and exploding gradients. Backpropagation computes \(\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=y_j-d_{kj}\) for \(j\in Y\), and for hidden neurons \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\,\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\,w_{rj}. \] Going down through the layers the derivative is repeatedly multiplied by factors \(\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\,w_{rj}\) (an explanation beyond the slide). If these factors are small, the gradient shrinks towards zero in the lower layers (vanishing); if they are large, it blows up (exploding).

Inexact gradient computation. The minibatch gradient is only an estimate of the true gradient. If \(s\) is the standard deviation of the gradient estimate from a single training example and \(b=\lvert T\rvert\) is the minibatch size, the standard deviation of the minibatch estimate is (roughly) \(s/\sqrt b\). E.g. minibatch size \(10\,000\) means 100 times more computation than size \(100\) but gives only \(10\) times less deviation (\(\sqrt{100}=10\)).

Minibatch size.
• Larger batches provide a more accurate estimate of the gradient, but with less than linear returns.
• Multicore architectures are usually underutilized by extremely small batches.
• If all examples in the batch are processed in parallel (the typical case), the amount of memory scales with the batch size – for many hardware setups this is the limiting factor.
• It is common (especially on GPUs) for power-of-2 batch sizes to offer better runtime; typical sizes range from 32 to 256, with 16 sometimes attempted for large models.
keyPoints: Repeated multiplication by \(\sigma_r'(\xi_r)w_{rj}\) → vanishing or exploding gradients
Minibatch gradient is only an estimate of the true gradient
Deviation of the estimate \(\approx s/\sqrt b\): 100× more computation gives only 10× less deviation
Larger batches: more accurate, less than linear returns, more memory
Small batches underuse multicore hardware; powers of 2 run faster (typically 32–256)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 109–110 (the mechanism of vanishing/exploding gradients is an elaboration; the slide calls s the "standard deviation of the gradient estimate for a single example")

name: Explain the momentum method: which problem of gradient descent does it address, what is the update formula, and how does SGD with momentum work? What is Nesterov momentum?
answer:
The issue: in gradient descent \( abla E(w^{(t)})\) constantly changes direction (while the error steadily decreases) – the descent zig-zags across elongated valleys.

Solution: in every step, add the change made in the previous step, weighted by a factor \(\alpha\): \[ \Delta w^{(t)}=-\varepsilon(t)\cdot rac1{\lvert T vert}\sum_{k\in T} abla E_k igl(w^{(t)} igr)+\alpha\,\Delta w^{(t-1)},\qquad 0\lt\alpha\lt1,\ \ \Delta w^{(-1)}=\vec 0. \] SGD with momentum: initialize \(w^{(0)}\) randomly close to 0; in step \(t+1\) choose (randomly) a minibatch \(T\subseteq\{1,\dots,p\}\) and compute \(w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}+\Delta w^{(t)}\) with \(\Delta w^{(t)}\) as above. Here \(0\lt\varepsilon(t)\le1\) is the learning rate, \(\alpha\) (typically 0.9) measures the "influence" of the momentum, and \( abla E_k(w^{(t)})\) is the gradient of the error of example \(k\). (The gradient is averaged over the minibatch, the same convention as in plain SGD.)

Intuition (interpretation): the update is a decaying sum of past gradients. Components of the gradient that keep changing sign cancel out, while components that consistently point in the same direction accumulate, so the trajectory oscillates less and moves faster along the valley – like a heavy ball rolling downhill.

Nesterov momentum: the gradient is evaluated at the look-ahead point \(w^{(t)}+\alpha\Delta w^{(t-1)}\) instead of at \(w^{(t)}\); it is the usual default in computer vision.
keyPoints: Problem: the gradient constantly changes direction (zig-zag)
\(\Delta w^{(t)}=-\varepsilon(t)\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\sum_{k\in T}\nabla E_k(w^{(t)})+\alpha\Delta w^{(t-1)}\)
\(0\lt\alpha\lt1\) = influence of the momentum (typically 0.9); \(\Delta w^{(-1)}=0\)
Previous update is added to the current gradient step
Oscillating components cancel, consistent ones accumulate
Nesterov: gradient evaluated at the look-ahead point
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 111–113 (the intuition paragraph is an interpretation)

name: How does one search for a good learning rate, and what is learning rate scheduling? Give the formulas of the power and exponential schedules and describe the warm-up / plateau / decay schedule.
answer:
Search for the learning rate.
• Use settings from a successful solution of a similar problem as a baseline.
• Search for the learning rate using learning monitoring: search through values from small (e.g. 0.001) to 0.1, possibly multiplying by 2; train for several epochs and observe the learning curves.

Scheduling: instead of a constant \(\varepsilon\), the learning rate \(\varepsilon(t)\) changes with the step \(t\) according to a fixed schedule.
• Power scheduling: \(\varepsilon(t)=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0}{1+t/s}\), where \(\varepsilon_0\) is the initial learning rate and \(s\) a constant number of steps. After \(s\) steps the rate is \(\varepsilon_0/2\), after \(2s\) it is \(\varepsilon_0/3\), etc.
• Exponential scheduling: \(\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon_0\cdot0.1^{t/s}\) – the rate drops by a factor of 10 every \(s\) steps, so it decays faster than power scheduling.
• Piecewise constant scheduling: a constant rate for a number of steps/epochs, then a smaller one, and so on.
• Warm-up, plateau, decay: increase the rate from zero linearly to \(\varepsilon_1\) early (about \(0.01T\) to \(0.05T\) steps, where \(T\) is the total number of steps), keep \(\varepsilon_1\) for most of the time (about \(0.8T\) to \(0.9T\)), then decrease linearly to \(\varepsilon_0\approx0.1\,\varepsilon_1\). Typically \(\varepsilon_1\) is between 0.01 and 0.1 for SGD and may scale with the batch size; the decay sometimes follows a half cosine curve. "Nothing is set in stone."

Example (derived). \(T=1000\), \(\varepsilon_1=0.1\), warm-up \(0.03T\), plateau until \(0.9T\): the rate rises from 0 to 0.1 during the first 30 steps, stays at 0.1 until step 900, then falls linearly to \(\varepsilon_0=0.01\) at step 1000.

Why schedule: a large rate at the beginning makes fast progress, a small rate at the end allows settling into a minimum instead of jumping around it; the short warm-up avoids unstable first steps.
keyPoints: Baseline from a similar solved problem
Try rates from about 0.001 to 0.1, multiplying by 2; watch learning curves
Power scheduling: \(\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon_0/(1+t/s)\)
Exponential scheduling: \(\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon_0\cdot0.1^{t/s}\)
Piecewise constant scheduling
Warm-up to \(\varepsilon_1\), long plateau, linear (or cosine) decay to about \(0.1\varepsilon_1\)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 117–118 (formulas and the warm-up/plateau/decay schedule; the numeric example is derived)

name: Explain AdaGrad: the motivation, the complete update formulas and the meaning of the constants. What is its main disadvantage?
answer:
Motivation. Fixed schedules use the same learning rate for all weights. It is better to have
• larger rates for weights whose gradients have been small so far,
• smaller rates for weights whose gradients have been large so far.
AdaGrad uses individually adapting learning rates for each weight, based on the accumulated squared gradients of the weight.

SGD with AdaGrad. Initialize \(w^{(0)}\) randomly close to 0 and \(r_{ji}^{(-1)}=0\). In step \(t+1\) choose (randomly) a minibatch \(T\subseteq\{1,\dots,p\}\), compute the minibatch gradient \[ g_{ji}^{(t)}=\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\sum_{k\in T}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr), \] and update \[ r_{ji}^{(t)}=r_{ji}^{(t-1)}+\bigl(g_{ji}^{(t)}\bigr)^2,\qquad w_{ji}^{(t+1)}=w_{ji}^{(t)}+\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)},\qquad\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}=-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{r_{ji}^{(t)}+\delta}}\;g_{ji}^{(t)}. \] • \(\eta\) is a constant expressing the influence of the learning rate, typically 0.01.
• \(\delta\gt0\) is a smoothing term (typically \(10^{-8}\)) avoiding division by 0.

How it works: \(r_{ji}\) accumulates the squares of all past minibatch gradients w.r.t. \(w_{ji}\). A weight with large gradients gets a large \(r_{ji}\) and hence a small effective rate \(\eta/\sqrt{r_{ji}+\delta}\); a weight with small gradients keeps a larger rate.

Main disadvantage: the squared gradients are accumulated throughout the whole learning process, so \(r_{ji}\) only grows and the effective learning rates only shrink. If the learning needs to get over several "hills" before settling in a deep "valley", the weight updates get far too small before getting there.
keyPoints: Individual learning rate for every weight
Larger rates for weights with small past gradients, smaller for large ones
\(r_{ji}^{(t)}=r_{ji}^{(t-1)}+(g_{ji}^{(t)})^2\), \(g\) = minibatch-average gradient
\(\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}=-\eta\,g_{ji}^{(t)}/\sqrt{r_{ji}^{(t)}+\delta}\)
\(\eta\approx0.01\); \(\delta\approx10^{-8}\) avoids division by zero
Disadvantage: accumulation over the whole history → updates become too small
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 119–120

name: Explain RMSProp: how does it fix the disadvantage of AdaGrad, what are its update formulas, and why are its first updates too large?
answer:
Idea. The main disadvantage of AdaGrad is the accumulation of squared gradients throughout the learning process. RMSProp uses an exponentially decaying average to discard history from the extreme past, so that it can converge rapidly after finding a convex bowl – as if it were an instance of AdaGrad initialized within that bowl.

SGD with RMSProp. Initialize \(w^{(0)}\) randomly close to 0 and \(r_{ji}^{(-1)}=0\). In step \(t+1\) choose a minibatch \(T\), compute \(g_{ji}^{(t)}=\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\sum_{k\in T}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}(w^{(t)})\) and \[ r_{ji}^{(t)}=\rho\,r_{ji}^{(t-1)}+(1-\rho)\bigl(g_{ji}^{(t)}\bigr)^2,\qquad\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}=-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{r_{ji}^{(t)}+\delta}}\;g_{ji}^{(t)},\qquad w_{ji}^{(t+1)}=w_{ji}^{(t)}+\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}. \] • \(\eta\) is a constant expressing the influence of the learning rate (Hinton suggests \(\rho=0.9\) and \(\eta=0.001\)); \(\delta\gt0\) is a smoothing term (typically \(10^{-8}\)).
The only difference from AdaGrad is the factor \(\rho\): old squared gradients are multiplied by \(\rho\) in every step and thus forgotten exponentially fast, so \(r_{ji}\) does not grow without bound.

Initial bias. Since \(r_{ji}^{(-1)}=0\), the first value is \(r_{ji}^{(0)}=(1-\rho)g^2\), so the first update is \(\approx-\eta\,g/\sqrt{(1-\rho)g^2}=-\dfrac{\eta}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\operatorname{sign}(g)\), i.e. about \(1/\sqrt{1-\rho}\approx3\) times larger than \(\eta\) for \(\rho=0.9\). Adam (next question) corrects this.
keyPoints: Exponentially decaying average discards the distant history
\(\Delta w_{ji}=-\eta\,g_{ji}/\sqrt{r_{ji}+\delta}\)
First updates too large by about \(1/\sqrt{1-\rho}\approx3\) because \(r\) starts at 0
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 121–122 (the size of the first update is derived from the slide's remark)

name: Explain Adam and AdamW: which two averages Adam keeps, why and how its bias correction works, what its update is, how AdamW differs from Adam with L2 regularization, and which optimizer is a good default.
answer:
Adam ("adaptive moment estimation") combines momentum with RMSProp. For every weight it keeps two exponentially decaying averages of the minibatch gradient \(g_{ji}^{(t)}\) (computed as in AdaGrad), starting from \(m_{ji}^{(-1)}=r_{ji}^{(-1)}=0\): \[ m_{ji}^{(t)}=\beta_1m_{ji}^{(t-1)}+(1-\beta_1)\,g_{ji}^{(t)},\qquad r_{ji}^{(t)}=\beta_2r_{ji}^{(t-1)}+(1-\beta_2)\bigl(g_{ji}^{(t)}\bigr)^2, \] the first moment (momentum) and the second moment (RMSProp).
Bias correction. Both averages start at 0, so in the first steps they are biased towards 0: e.g. \(r^{(0)}=(1-\beta_2)g^2\) with \(1-\beta_2=0.001\) would make the first updates about 30 times too large (dividing by \(\sqrt{0.001}\)). Adam divides by the factors \(1-\beta_1^{t+1}\) and \(1-\beta_2^{t+1}\), which tend to 1 as \(t\) grows: \[ \hat m_{ji}^{(t)}=\frac{m_{ji}^{(t)}}{1-\beta_1^{t+1}},\qquad\hat r_{ji}^{(t)}=\frac{r_{ji}^{(t)}}{1-\beta_2^{t+1}},\qquad\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}=-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\hat r_{ji}^{(t)}}+\delta}\;\hat m_{ji}^{(t)},\qquad w_{ji}^{(t+1)}=w_{ji}^{(t)}+\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}. \] Typical constants: \(\eta=0.001\), \(\beta_1=0.9\), \(\beta_2=0.999\), \(\delta=10^{-8}\). Net effect: every update has size roughly \(\eta\), independently of the scale of the gradients, and its direction is smoothed by the momentum. (Check at \(t=0\): \(\hat m=g\), \(\hat r=g^2\), so \(\Delta w\approx-\eta\,\operatorname{sign}(g)\).)

AdamW. With adaptive learning rates L2 regularization and weight decay are not equivalent: L2 adds \(\zeta w_{ji}/\eta\) to the gradient, and Adam then divides everything by \(\sqrt{\hat r_{ji}}+\delta\), so weights with large gradients are hardly regularized at all. AdamW decouples the decay from the gradient: the weights are decayed directly and the Adam update uses the gradient of \(E\) only: \[ w_{ji}^{(t+1)}=(1-\zeta)\,w_{ji}^{(t)}+\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}. \] In libraries \(\zeta=\eta\lambda\) with the "weight decay" parameter \(\lambda\) (typically 0.01–0.1), so the decay follows the learning rate schedule.

Which optimizer? Adam/AdamW is the default in most of today's deep learning; essentially all transformers and large language models use AdamW with a warm-up schedule and gradient clipping. SGD with (Nesterov) momentum is still standard for convolutional networks in computer vision (often generalizes slightly better, but needs more careful learning-rate tuning); RMSProp and AdaGrad are mostly of historical interest. Rule of thumb: start with AdamW with default parameters and a warm-up schedule, tune the learning rate first.
keyPoints: Adam keeps \(m\) (average of gradients, momentum) and \(r\) (average of squared gradients, RMSProp)
Bias correction: \(\hat m=m/(1-\beta_1^{t+1})\), \(\hat r=r/(1-\beta_2^{t+1})\) fixes the bias of the zero start
\(\Delta w=-\eta\,\hat m/(\sqrt{\hat r}+\delta)\); typically \(\eta=0.001\), \(\beta_1=0.9\), \(\beta_2=0.999\)
Update size roughly η independent of the gradient scale
AdamW decouples decay: \(w\leftarrow(1-\zeta)w+\Delta w\); L2 inside Adam barely regularizes weights with large gradients
Default: AdamW with warm-up and clipping; SGD + Nesterov momentum for CNNs
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 123–125 and 152 (the first-step check is derived)

name: Explain gradient clipping: which problem it addresses, what the clipped gradient is, how clipping by norm differs from clipping by value, and compute the clipped gradient for \(g=(3,4)\) with threshold \(c=1\) and for \(c=10\).
answer:
Problem. Recall steep cliffs: a single minibatch gradient may be huge, and one step of the descent throws the weights far away from the region where the descent was making progress. This is typical for recurrent networks and transformers, where long products of Jacobians appear in backpropagation (exploding gradients).

Solution: keep the direction of the gradient but cap its length. If the norm of the minibatch gradient \(g\) exceeds a threshold \(c\gt0\), rescale \(g\) to norm \(c\): \[ g\;\longmapsto\;\min\Bigl\{1,\frac{c}{\lVert g\rVert}\Bigr\}\,g,\qquad g=\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\sum_{k\in T}\nabla E_k\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr). \] \(\lVert g\rVert\) is the norm of the whole gradient vector (over all weights). The clipped gradient is then used in the update of whatever algorithm is used: SGD, \(w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}-\varepsilon(t)\,g\), momentum, Adam, … Typical thresholds: \(c=1\) for transformers, larger (e.g. \(c=5\)) for recurrent networks.

Norm vs. value. A cruder variant clips every component of \(g\) separately to \([-c,c]\) ("clipping by value"); this changes the direction of the gradient. Clipping by norm multiplies the whole vector by one scalar, so the direction is preserved – it is the standard.

Example. \(g=(3,4)\), \(\lVert g\rVert=\sqrt{9+16}=5\).
• \(c=1\): \(\min\{1,1/5\}=0.2\), clipped gradient \(0.2\cdot(3,4)=(0.6,0.8)\), whose norm is \(1=c\) and whose direction is unchanged.
• \(c=10\): \(\lVert g\rVert=5\le c\), so the factor is \(\min\{1,2\}=1\) and \(g\) is unchanged.
(Clipping by value with \(c=1\) would give \((1,1)\) – a different direction.)
keyPoints: Exploding gradient / steep cliff throws the weights far away; typical for RNNs and transformers
Clip by norm: \(g\mapsto\min\{1,c/\lVert g\rVert\}\,g\) – keeps the direction, caps the length at \(c\)
Clipped gradient is used in any optimizer (SGD, momentum, Adam)
Clipping by value changes the direction; by norm is the standard
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 114–115 (the numeric example is derived)

name: What generic requirements are imposed on (hidden) activation functions, and why and how are inputs preprocessed before training?
answer:
Generic requirements on activation functions:
1. Differentiability – to do gradient descent.
2. Non-linearity – linear multi-layer networks are equivalent to single-layer ones.
3. Monotonicity – local extrema of activation functions induce local extrema of the error function.
4. "Linearity" – preserve as much linearity as possible; linear models are easiest to fit; find the "minimum" non-linearity needed to solve the given task.
The choice of activation functions is closely related to input preprocessing and the initial choice of weights.

Input preprocessing.
• Some inputs may be much larger than others – e.g. the height vs. the weight of a person, the maximum speed of a car (in km/h) vs. its price (in CZK).
• Large inputs have a greater influence on the training than the small ones. Also, too large inputs may slow down learning (saturation of some activation functions).
• Typical standardization (per input component): average 0 (subtract the mean) and variance 1 (divide by the standard deviation). The mean and the standard deviation may be estimated from the training set.
keyPoints: Differentiability (needed for gradient descent)
Non-linearity (linear multilayer nets collapse to a single layer)
Monotonicity (extrema of σ induce extrema of the error)
"Linearity": as close to linear as the task allows
Inputs of different scales: large ones dominate and may saturate activations
Standardize: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation (estimated on the training set)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 126–127

name: Explain the intuition behind weight initialization and derive the normal LeCun initialization, including the proof that \(\mathrm{Var}[\xi]=n\,s^2\). (Convention: in \(N(\mu,v)\) the second argument is the variance.)
answer:
Intuition. Assume the weights are chosen randomly – from what distribution? Consider the behaviour of a deep network: small weights make the values of inner potentials vanish, large weights make them explode. Hence we want to choose the weights so that the inner potentials of neurons are stable (similar in all layers of the network).

Normal LeCun initialization. Assume the input data have mean 0 and variance 1. Consider a neuron \(j\) from the first layer with \(n\) inputs (fan-in \(n\)), and assume its weights are chosen randomly from the normal distribution \(N(0,s^2)\) (standard deviation \(s\)), all random choices being independent.
The rule: choose \(s\) so that the standard deviation of \(\xi_j\) satisfies \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\xi_j]}\approx1\).
Basic properties of the variance of independent variables give \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\xi_j]}=\sqrt n\,s\). Thus by putting \(s=\sqrt{1/n}\) we obtain standard deviation 1. The same works for higher layers; \(n\) then corresponds to the number of neurons in the layer one level lower. This gives \[ w_i\sim N\!\left(0,\tfrac1n\right). \] Derivation. Consider a single neuron without bias with inner potential \(\xi=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_ix_i\). Consider all \(w_i\) and \(x_i\) as independent random variables (so \(\xi\) is also a random variable), where
• \(w_i\sim N(0,s^2)\) for \(i=1,\dots,n\), \(s\) a constant,
• \(\mathbb E[x_i]=0\) and \(\mathrm{Var}[x_i]=\mathbb E[(x_i-\mathbb E x_i)^2]=1\).
We prove \(\mathrm{Var}[\xi]=n\,s^2\):
1. \(\mathbb E[\xi]=\sum_i\mathbb E[w_ix_i]=\sum_i\mathbb E[w_i]\,\mathbb E[x_i]=0\) (independence).
2. \(\mathrm{Var}[w_ix_i]=\mathbb E[w_i^2x_i^2]-\mathbb E[w_ix_i]^2=\mathbb E[w_i^2]\,\mathbb E[x_i^2]-0=s^2\cdot1\), because \(\mathbb E[w_i^2]=\mathrm{Var}[w_i]=s^2\) and \(\mathbb E[x_i^2]=\mathrm{Var}[x_i]=1\) (both have zero mean).
3. \(\mathrm{Var}[\xi]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Var}[w_ix_i]=n\,s^2\) (independence).
Therefore the standard deviation of \(\xi\) is \(\sqrt n\,s\), and requiring it to be 1 gives \(s^2=1/n\).
keyPoints: Small weights → potentials vanish; large weights → potentials explode; want stable potentials
Inputs standardized (mean 0, variance 1); weights \(\sim N(0,s^2)\), independent
\(\mathbb E[\xi]=0\) by independence
\(\mathrm{Var}[w_ix_i]=\mathbb E[w_i^2]\mathbb E[x_i^2]=s^2\)
\(\mathrm{Var}[\xi]=n\,s^2\) → set \(s^2=1/n\)
Normal LeCun: \(w_i\sim N(0,1/n)\), \(n\) = fan-in of the neuron
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 128–130 (the second argument of N is the variance; the symbol s for the standard deviation replaces the slide's w)

name: Describe the normal and uniform Glorot (Xavier) initializations and the uniform LeCun initialization (fan-in \(n\), fan-out \(m\)). What does Glorot add to LeCun's reasoning? Derive the bound of the uniform LeCun variant.
answer:
Normal Glorot initialization. The LeCun heuristic ignores the variance of the gradient – it is concerned only with the "size" of activations in the forward pass. Glorot & Bengio (2010) chose the weights randomly from \[ N\!\left(0,\frac{2}{m+n}\right)=N\!\left(0,\frac1{(m+n)/2}\right), \] where \(n\) is the number of inputs to the layer (fan-in) and \(m\) is the number of neurons in the layer above (fan-out). It is designed as a compromise between the goal of initializing all layers to have the same activation variance (which asks for variance \(1/n\)) and the goal of initializing all layers to have the same gradient variance (which asks for \(1/m\)). This gives the normal Glorot (normal Xavier) initialization \(w_i\sim N(0,\tfrac{2}{m+n})\).

Uniform variants. The weights are drawn from \(U(-a,a)\) with \(a\) chosen so that the variance is the same as in the normal case. The variance of \(U(-a,a)\) is \(a^2/3\).
• Uniform LeCun: inputs with mean 0 and variance 1, neuron with \(n\) inputs: \(\mathrm{Var}[\xi]=n\cdot\frac{a^2}{3}\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{n/3}\,a\). Setting it to 1 gives \(a=\sqrt{3/n}\), i.e. \(w_i\sim U\bigl(-\sqrt{3/n},\sqrt{3/n}\bigr)\).
• Uniform Glorot: replace \(n\) by \((m+n)/2\): \(w_i\sim U\bigl(-\sqrt{6/(m+n)},\sqrt{6/(m+n)}\bigr)\), because \(a^2/3=2/(m+n)\) gives \(a^2=6/(m+n)\).
keyPoints: LeCun considers only forward-pass activation variance
Glorot: compromise between equal activation variance and equal gradient variance
Normal Glorot: \(w_i\sim N(0,\frac{2}{m+n})\), \(n\) fan-in, \(m\) fan-out
Variance of \(U(-a,a)\) is \(a^2/3\) → uniform LeCun \(a=\sqrt{3/n}\)
Uniform Glorot: \(a=\sqrt{6/(m+n)}\)

name: Characterise ReLU and at least one of its modern variants as hidden activation functions: formulas, advantages and problems.
answer:
ReLU. For hidden neurons, sigmoidal functions are often substituted with piece-wise linear activations; the most prominent is ReLU, \(\sigma(\xi)=\max\{0,\xi\}\).
• THE default activation function recommended for most feedforward neural networks.
• As close to a linear function as possible; very simple; does not saturate for large potentials.
• Dead for negative potentials (zero output and zero gradient).

Variants (one is enough).
• Leaky ReLU: generalizes ReLU with a small slope for negative potentials, so it is not dead there; experimentally not much better than ReLU.
• ELU ("smoothed" ReLU): \(\sigma(\xi)=\alpha(e^{\xi}-1)\) for \(\xi\lt0\) and \(\sigma(\xi)=\xi\) for \(\xi\ge0\), where \(\alpha\) is a parameter; ELU converges to \(-\alpha\) as \(\xi\to-\infty\). As opposed to ReLU: smooth, always non-zero gradient (but saturates), slower to compute.
• SELU: a scaled variant of ELU, \(\sigma(\xi)=\lambda\cdot\mathrm{ELU}(\xi)\), self-normalizing: for suitable constants \(\lambda,\alpha\), properly initialized weights and normalized inputs the output of each layer tends to preserve mean close to 0 and standard deviation close to 1.
keyPoints: ReLU \(\max\{0,\xi\}\): default, nearly linear, no saturation for large potentials, dead for negative ones
ELU: \(\alpha(e^\xi-1)\) for \(\xi\lt0\), \(\xi\) otherwise – smooth, non-zero gradient, saturates at \(-\alpha\), slower
Leaky ReLU: small slope for negative potentials, not dead
SELU = scaled ELU, self-normalizing (mean ≈ 0, std ≈ 1)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 139–144 (not in the 2026 deck; slide 142 is a plot)

name: Why is LeCun initialization not justified for ReLU, and what does He initialization do instead? Derive the He variance \(2/n\) (fan-in \(n\)) and state which initialization is matched to which activation.
answer:
Problem. ReLU is not as sensitive to a large variance of the inner potential as sigmoidal functions, but it is still good to keep the variance constant (at least because of the output layer). LeCun's derivation needs the outputs of the previous layer to have zero mean and unit variance. ReLU is not a symmetric function, so even if the inner potential \(\xi\) has variance 1, this is not true of its output \(y=\max\{0,\xi\}\): the second moment is halved.

Derivation (derived, the slides only state the result). Let the potentials \(\xi\) of the previous layer be symmetric around 0 with variance \(v\). By symmetry \[ \mathbb E[y^2]=\mathbb E\bigl[\xi^2\,\mathbf 1_{\xi\gt0}\bigr]=\tfrac12\,\mathbb E[\xi^2]=\tfrac12\,v. \] The next potential is \(\xi'=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iy_i\) with independent weights \(w_i\sim N(0,s^2)\), independent of the \(y_i\). Then \(\mathbb E[w_iy_i]=0\) and \[ \mathrm{Var}[\xi']=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb E[w_i^2]\,\mathbb E[y_i^2]=n\,s^2\cdot\tfrac12\,v. \] Requiring \(\mathrm{Var}[\xi']=v\) (stable potentials) gives \(s^2=2/n\). So the weight variance is doubled compared with LeCun: \[ \text{normal He: }\ w_i\sim N\!\left(0,\tfrac2n\right)\qquad(\text{LeCun: }N(0,\tfrac1n)). \] Matching initialization to activation (rule of thumb). Glorot for sigmoidal activations (tanh, logistic, softmax outputs), He for ReLU and its variants, LeCun for SELU. All are available in deep learning libraries (the exact table need not be memorised).
keyPoints: ReLU is not symmetric: the second moment of the output is half of the potential's variance
\(\mathbb E[\mathrm{ReLU}(\xi)^2]=\frac12\mathrm{Var}[\xi]\) for symmetric \(\xi\) with mean 0
\(\mathrm{Var}[\xi']=n\,s^2\cdot\frac12 v\) → \(s^2=2/n\)
Normal He: \(w_i\sim N(0,2/n)\) (LeCun: \(N(0,1/n)\))
Glorot for sigmoidal activations, He for ReLU and variants, LeCun for SELU
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 132 (He initialization and rule of thumb; the derivation and the SELU assignment from older slides 139–144 are flagged as derived/older)

name: Explain batch normalization (roughly): the intuition, the computation during training with formulas, the trainable parameters, and what is done during inference. Then normalize the potentials of a layer with \(q=2\) neurons over a minibatch of \(p=3\) examples \(z_1=(1,10)\), \(z_2=(1,40)\), \(z_3=(4,40)\) with \(\delta=0\).
answer:
Intuition. Instead of keeping mean 0 and variance 1 only implicitly through a clever weight initialization, we may renormalize the inner potentials of neurons throughout the layers. The inner potentials of the \(\ell\)-th layer are the inputs to the sub-network consisting of the activation functions of the \(\ell\)-th layer and all layers above – so standardize them just as we did with the input data. For this we need a "dataset" of potentials of the \(\ell\)-th layer; a (mini)batch provides it.

Training. Consider the \(\ell\)-th layer with \(n\) neurons and a batch of \(p\) training examples.
1. For every \(k=1,\dots,p\) compute the inner potentials of the neurons of the \(\ell\)-th layer for the input \(x_k\): \(z_k=(z_{k1},\dots,z_{kn})\).
2. Normalize every component across the batch: \[ \hat z_{ki}=\frac{z_{ki}-\mu_i}{s_i},\quad\mu_i=\frac1p\sum_{k=1}^{p}z_{ki},\quad s_i=\sqrt{\frac1p\sum_{k=1}^{p}(z_{ki}-\mu_i)^2+\delta}, \] where \(\delta\gt0\) is a small smoothing term.
3. Use \(\gamma_i\hat z_{ki}+\beta_i\) as the inner potential of neuron \(i\) instead of \(z_{ki}\), i.e. the neuron outputs \(\sigma_i(\gamma_i\hat z_{ki}+\beta_i)\). Here \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are new trainable weights (initially \(\gamma_i=1\), \(\beta_i=0\)); the network can even undo the normalization with \(\gamma_i=s_i\), \(\beta_i=\mu_i\).

Inference. For a single input there is no batch to compute statistics from; we use the running averages of \(\mu_i\) and \(s_i\) (exponentially decaying averages of their minibatch values) collected during training.

Worked example (\(\delta=0\)). Neuron 1: values \(1,1,4\), \(\mu_1=2\), variance \(\frac13(1+1+4)=2\), \(s_1=\sqrt2\); \(\hat z_{\cdot1}=\bigl(-\tfrac1{\sqrt2},-\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\sqrt2\bigr)\approx(-0.71,-0.71,1.41)\) – mean 0 and variance \(\frac13(\frac12+\frac12+2)=1\).
Neuron 2: values \(10,40,40\), \(\mu_2=30\), variance \(\frac13(400+100+100)=200\), \(s_2=10\sqrt2\); \(\hat z_{\cdot2}=\bigl(-\sqrt2,\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigr)\approx(-1.41,0.71,0.71)\).
So \(\hat z_1\approx(-0.71,-1.41)\), \(\hat z_2\approx(-0.71,0.71)\), \(\hat z_3\approx(1.41,0.71)\): both neurons now have mean 0 and variance 1 and are on the same scale although neuron 2 worked on a ten times larger scale.
keyPoints: Explicitly renormalize inner potentials instead of relying on initialization
Potentials of layer ℓ are inputs of the sub-network above it
Per neuron over the batch: \(\hat z_{ki}=(z_{ki}-\mu_i)/s_i\) with batch mean \(\mu_i\) and \(s_i=\sqrt{\text{variance}+\delta}\)
Neuron outputs \(\sigma_i(\gamma_i\hat z_{ki}+\beta_i)\) with trainable \(\gamma,\beta\) (initially 1, 0)
Inference: running averages of μ_i and s_i collected during training
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 133–137 (slides give the formulas and the example; slide 135 uses s_i with δ inside the root)

name: What is generalization and why is regularization "a big issue" in neural networks? Explain early stopping, including the data split and the possible stopping rules.
answer:
Generalization = the ability to cope with new, unseen instances. Data are mostly noisy, so it is not good to fit them exactly; in function approximation the network should not return exactly the results from the training set. More formally, it is typically assumed that the training set has been generated as \[ d_{kj}=g_j(x_k)+\Theta_{kj}, \] where \(g_j\) is the "underlying" function corresponding to the output neuron \(j\in Y\) and \(\Theta_{kj}\) is random noise. The network should fit \(g_j\), not the noise. Methods improving generalization are called regularization methods.

Why a big issue: neural networks typically use a huge number of parameters and are thus very susceptible to overfitting (the quip "with four parameters I can fit an elephant" makes the point).

Early stopping means that we stop learning before it reaches a minimum of the error \(E\). Reasons:
• in many applications the error function is not the main thing we want to optimize (e.g. a trading system should maximize profit, not minimize a strange error function designed to be easily differentiable);
• minimizing \(E\) completely is not good for generalization.
Standard approach: train on one set and stop on another one. Divide the dataset into
• a training set (e.g. 60 %) – train the network here,
• a validation set (e.g. 20 %) – use it to stop the training,
• a test set (e.g. 20 %) – use it to evaluate the final model.

Stopping rules:
• observe \(E\) (or any other function of interest) on the validation set; if it has not improved for the last \(q\) steps, stop;
• alternatively, observe the gradient; if it is small for some time, stop. (Some studies have shown that this traditional rule is not too good – the gradient may be larger close to minimum values; on the other hand, \(E\) does not have to be evaluated, which saves time.)
To compare models one may use ML techniques such as various types of cross-validation.
keyPoints: Generalization = coping with unseen instances; fit \(g_j\), not the noise (\(d_{kj}=g_j(x_k)+\Theta_{kj}\))
Many parameters → overfitting; regularization = methods improving generalization
Early stopping: stop before reaching the minimum of E
Training / validation / test sets (e.g. 60/20/20)
Stop when the validation error has not improved for the last \(q\) steps
Alternative: stop on a small gradient (cheaper but less reliable)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 138–140 and 144–145

name: How should the size of a network be chosen? What are the symptoms of a network that is too small or too large, and what do the hidden neurons of a small two-layer network represent?
answer:
Size of the network – a similar problem as with the training duration:
• a too small network is not able to capture the intrinsic properties of the training set (underfitting);
• large networks overfit faster.
"Solution": the optimal number of neurons – but
• there are some (useless) theoretical bounds;
• there are algorithms dynamically adding/removing neurons (not much used nowadays);
• in practice: start with an existing network solving a similar problem. If you are truly desperate, solving a brand new problem, you may try an ancient rule of thumb: the number of neurons \(\approx\) ten times less than the number of training instances (e.g. 1000 training examples \(\to\) about 100 neurons).
• Experiment, experiment, experiment.

Feature extraction. In a two-layer network (one hidden layer) the hidden neurons are supposed to represent "patterns" in the inputs: each hidden neuron has a weight vector over the inputs and fires when its pattern is present. With very few hidden neurons the network must compress the input into a few task-relevant features – e.g. in a \(64\)-\(2\)-\(3\) network that classifies noisy \(8\times8\) pixel images of three letters, the two hidden neurons can learn two stroke patterns that together are sufficient for the output layer to tell the three letters apart (this concrete example is an interpretation).
keyPoints: Too small: cannot capture the properties of the training set (underfitting)
Too large: overfits faster
Theoretical bounds are useless; dynamic adding/removing of neurons is not used much
Practice: start from an existing network for a similar problem and experiment
Rule of thumb: neurons \(\approx\) number of training instances / 10
Hidden neurons represent patterns (features) of the inputs
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 146–147 (the letter example is an interpretation of the slide's 64-2-3 figure)

name: Explain ensemble methods and bagging: why do ensembles reduce the generalization error, how are the training sets generated, how are the models combined, and what fraction of distinct examples does a bootstrap sample contain on average?
answer:
Ensemble methods are techniques for reducing the generalization error by combining several models. They work because different models will usually not make all the same errors on the test set. Idea: train several different models separately, then have all of the models vote on the output for test examples.

Bagging:
• generate \(B\) training sets \(T_1,\dots,T_B\) by sampling from \(T\) uniformly with replacement (each of size \(\lvert T\rvert\));
• for each \(i\), train a model \(M_i\) on \(T_i\);
• combine the outputs of the models: for regression by averaging, for classification by (majority) voting.

Distinct examples in a sample. A fixed example is missed by one draw with probability \(1-\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\), so it is missed by all \(\lvert T\rvert\) draws with probability \(\bigl(1-\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\bigr)^{\lvert T\rvert}\to\frac1e\). Hence on average \(\lvert T_i\rvert_{\text{distinct}}\approx\bigl(1-\frac1e\bigr)\lvert T\rvert\approx0.63\,\lvert T\rvert\) distinct examples.

Cost: each model is trained to convergence on its own training set, which is infeasible for large networks and training sets – the motivation for dropout (next question).
keyPoints: Ensembles: different models make different errors; combine by averaging/voting
Bagging: B training sets sampled with replacement, one model per set
A bootstrap sample contains on average \((1-1/e)\lvert T\rvert\approx0.63\lvert T\rvert\) distinct examples
Regression: average; classification: majority vote
Training many large networks to convergence is expensive
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 148 (the 1-1/e limit is derived)

name: Explain dropout: the algorithm, its formal description via inner potentials (with the drop probability \(\pi\)), why the surviving values are scaled, its relation to bagging, and what happens during inference.
answer:
The algorithm. In every step of the gradient descent
• choose randomly a set of neurons, each neuron being kept independently with probability \(1-\pi\) (\(\pi=\frac12\) in the basic version; in practice different probabilities are used as well);
• do the forward and backward propagation only using the selected neurons (the weights of the other neurons are left unchanged).

Formally. Without dropout \(\xi_j=\sum_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}w_{ji}y_i\). With dropout (neurons are dropped with probability \(\pi\)) draw \[ r_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1-\pi)\ \text{ for all } i\in j_{\leftarrow}\setminus\{0\},\quad r_0=1,\qquad \xi_j=\sum_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}w_{ji}\,\frac{r_i}{1-\pi}\,y_i. \] Randomly chosen neurons are masked out (the bias input \(0\) never); the values of the remaining neurons are scaled by \(\frac1{1-\pi}\), i.e. doubled for \(\pi=\frac12\).

Why the scaling. \(\mathbb E\bigl[\frac{r_i}{1-\pi}\bigr]=1\), so the expected potential during training equals the potential with all neurons present: \(\mathbb E[\xi_j]=\sum_iw_{ji}y_i\).

Inference. Nothing is dropped and nothing is scaled. (This is "inverted dropout", used by all libraries; the original paper instead scales by \(1-\pi\) at inference, which is equivalent.)

Relation to bagging. Dropout resembles bagging: a large ensemble of neural networks is trained "at once" on parts of the data. It is not exactly the same: the models share parameters, each model inheriting a different subset of parameters from the parent network. This sharing makes it possible to represent an exponential number of models with a tractable amount of memory, whereas in bagging each model is trained to convergence on its own training set, which would be infeasible for large networks.
keyPoints: Each step: keep each neuron with probability \(1-\pi\), propagate only through kept neurons
\(\xi_j=\sum_i w_{ji}\frac{r_i}{1-\pi}y_i\), \(r_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1-\pi)\), \(r_0=1\) (bias never dropped)
Scaling by \(1/(1-\pi)\) keeps \(\mathbb E[\xi_j]\) equal to the full potential
Inference: nothing dropped, nothing scaled (inverted dropout)
Like bagging, but exponentially many sub-models share parameters
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 149–150 (expectation check derived)

name: Explain weight decay and L2 regularization, and prove that weight decay is equivalent to gradient descent (with a constant learning rate) on an error function with an L2 penalty. Why is this equivalence not valid for adaptive optimizers?
answer:
Idea. Generalization can be improved by removing "unimportant" weights. Penalising large weights gives a stronger indication about their importance.

Weight decay. In every step we decrease the weights (multiplicatively): \[ w_{ji}^{(t+1)}=(1-\zeta)\,w_{ji}^{(t)}-\varepsilon\,\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr). \] Intuition: unimportant weights will be pushed to 0, important weights will survive the decay (the gradient term keeps restoring them).

Equivalence. Weight decay is equivalent to gradient descent with a constant learning rate \(\varepsilon\) on the error function \[ E'(w)=E(w)+\frac{\zeta}{2\varepsilon}\,(w\cdot w),\qquad w\cdot w=\sum_{j,i}w_{ji}^2, \] where \(\frac{\zeta}{2\varepsilon}(w\cdot w)\) is the L2 regularization term that penalizes large weights.

Proof. Differentiate \(E'\) w.r.t. a weight: \(\dfrac{\partial E'}{\partial w_{ji}}=\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}+\dfrac{\zeta}{2\varepsilon}\cdot2w_{ji}=\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}+\dfrac{\zeta}{\varepsilon}\,w_{ji}\). A gradient descent step on \(E'\) with learning rate \(\varepsilon\) gives \[ w_{ji}^{(t+1)}=w_{ji}^{(t)}-\varepsilon\frac{\partial E'}{\partial w_{ji}}\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr)=w_{ji}^{(t)}-\varepsilon\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr)-\zeta\,w_{ji}^{(t)}=(1-\zeta)\,w_{ji}^{(t)}-\varepsilon\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr), \] which is exactly the weight decay update. \(\square\)

Remark. The equivalence holds for plain gradient descent with a constant learning rate only. With adaptive learning rates (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam) the L2 term is rescaled together with the gradient, and weight decay applied directly to the weights (AdamW) is the one to use.
keyPoints: Remove unimportant weights by penalising large weights
Weight decay: \(w^{(t+1)}=(1-\zeta)w^{(t)}-\varepsilon\,\partial E/\partial w\)
Equivalent error: \(E'(w)=E(w)+\frac{\zeta}{2\varepsilon}(w\cdot w)\)
\(\partial E'/\partial w_{ji}=\partial E/\partial w_{ji}+\frac\zeta\varepsilon w_{ji}\)
GD step on \(E'\) with rate \(\varepsilon\) reproduces the decay factor \((1-\zeta)\)
Equivalence only for plain GD with constant rate; adaptive optimizers use decoupled decay (AdamW)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 151–152 (the differentiation step spells out the stated equivalence)
